content: A cathode is an electrode through which positive electric current exits a polarized electrical device. This is often remembered using the mnemonic CCD (Cathode Current Departs). Contrary to a common misconception, the polarity of a cathode is not always negative. Its polarity depends on the type of device and its mode of operation, as defined by the direction of current flow. For example: In a discharging battery or galvanic cell, the cathode is the positive terminal where conventional current flows out. Internally, this outward current is carried by positive ions moving from the electrolyte to the positive cathode, driven by chemical energy. Externally, electrons move inward, creating a flow of negative charge in one direction and positive current in the opposite direction. In a recharging battery or an electrolytic cell, the cathode is the negative terminal, which sends current back to the external generator. In a diode, the cathode is the negative terminal at the pointed end of the arrow symbol, where current exits the device. The naming of electrodes in diodes is based on the direction of forward current (the direction in which current flows most easily), even for devices like Zener diodes or solar cells where the reverse current is of interest. An electrode through which current flows into the device is called an anode. Etymology The term cathode was coined in 1834 by William Whewell, who was consulted by Michael Faraday for naming conventions in his work on electrolysis. The word derives from the Greek κάθοδος (kathodos), meaning descent or way down. Faraday explained that in an electrolytic cell oriented so that current flows from east to west (or in the direction the sun appears to move), the cathode is where the current exits the electrolyte, on the west side. This naming convention was chosen to be independent of any future changes in the current direction convention, which was not fully understood at the time. Faraday initially used the term exode (meaning the exit point for current) but changed it to cathode to align with the idea of the west electrode. This decision was based on the Earth's magnetic field direction, which was then believed to be invariant. However, the Earth's magnetic field is now known to reverse periodically, making the term cathode less intuitive than exode. Despite this, the term cathode has persisted, and a more modern interpretation links it to the flow of electrons into the device. Chemistry In chemistry, a cathode is the electrode at which reduction occurs, meaning electrons are added to cations to complete their valence shells or form bonds. The cathode can be either negative or positive, depending on whether the cell is electrolytic or galvanic. In a galvanic cell, the cathode is positive, even though it might be expected to repel positively charged cations. This is due to differences in electrode potential relative to the electrolyte solution. Electrolytic Cell In an electrolytic cell, the cathode is the electrode where negative polarity is applied to drive the cell. Common reduction reactions at the cathode include the production of hydrogen gas or pure metal from metal ions. Galvanic Cell In a galvanic cell, the cathode is the electrode connected to the positive pole, completing the circuit. Electrons released by the anode return to the cell through the cathode. Electroplating During electroplating, metal ions in an ionic solution are reduced at the cathode, forming a pure metal surface. Objects to be plated are attached to the cathode in the electrolytic solution. Electronics and Physics In physics and electronics, a cathode is an electrode that emits electrons into a device. Vacuum Tubes In vacuum tubes, the cathode emits free electrons. These electrons are extracted from metal electrodes either by heating (thermionic emission) or by applying a strong electric field (field emission). Electrons can also be emitted via the photoelectric effect when light of sufficient frequency strikes the electrode. Cold and Hot Cathodes Cathodes used for field emission in vacuum tubes are called cold cathodes. Heated electrodes, or hot cathodes (often referred to as filaments), are more common. Hot cathodes were widely used in radios and televisions before the 1970s and are still used in cathode ray tubes for television sets and computer monitors. They are also used as electrodes in fluorescent lamps and X-ray source tubes. Diodes In a semiconductor diode, the cathode is the N-doped layer of the PN junction. Initially, the N-doped layer supplies electrons to the junction, which combine with holes from the P-doped layer. This creates a depleted zone at the junction, leaving a thin layer of positive ions in the cathode, giving it a base positive charge. When a negative charge is applied to the cathode, more N-doped ions supply electrons to the junction, making the diode conductive and allowing electron flow from the cathode to the anode. In Zener diodes, the cathode remains fixed but can conduct current in the reverse direction if the breakdown or Zener voltage is exceeded.
